title: The projection matrix
objectives: Build the matrix that projects onto a column space.

screens.prose: The line runs along $\mathbf{a} = (3, 4)$. Drag $\mathbf{b}$ anywhere: the projection $\mathbf{p}$ follows, and the caption shows both.
screens.question: Put $\mathbf{b}$ at $(2, 1)$, then at $(4, 2)$. What happens to $\mathbf{p}$ when $\mathbf{b}$ doubles?

options.why: That happens when you double $\mathbf{a}$, which keeps the line. Doubling $\mathbf{b}$ moved $\mathbf{p}$ from $(1.2, 1.6)$ to $(2.4, 3.2)$.
Only $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$ changes, and it doubles. Read the caption at $(2, 1)$ and $(4, 2)$.
$\mathbf{p}$ always lies on the line through $\mathbf{a}$. Only its length changes.

hints.text: Read $\mathbf{p}$ in the caption at both positions and compare.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read $\mathbf{p}$ in the caption at $(2, 1)$ and at $(4, 2)$.

explain.text: Doubling $\mathbf{b}$ doubles $\mathbf{p}$, and adding two $\mathbf{b}$'s adds their $\mathbf{p}$'s. So projection is linear, and a linear map is a matrix. In the caption, each coordinate of $\mathbf{p}$ is a fixed mix of $\mathbf{b}$'s coordinates.

screens.prose: A matrix is fixed by where it sends $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$: those are its columns. Project both onto the line through $\mathbf{a} = (3, 4)$, using $\mathbf{p} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{25}\,\mathbf{a}$.
screens.question: Fill in the two projections.

hints.text: For $\mathbf{b} = (1, 0)$, $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 3$.
So $\mathbf{p} = \tfrac{3}{25}(3, 4)$. For $(0, 1)$, $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each $\mathbf{b}$, find $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$, divide by 25, then scale $(3, 4)$.

byKey.r1c1: Here $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 4$, so the first coordinate is $\tfrac{4}{25} \times 3 = 0.48$.

screens.prose: Your two answers are the columns of $\mathbf{P}$, the **projection matrix** onto the line. Try it on $\mathbf{b} = (5, 10)$ from the last lesson.
screens.question: Compute $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{b}$.

hints.text: Each entry is a row of P dotted with b.
First entry: $0.36 \times 5 + 0.48 \times 10$.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{b} = (6.6, 8.8)$, the projection you found by dragging.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot each row of $\mathbf{P}$ with $\mathbf{b} = (5, 10)$.

explain.text: One matrix does every projection onto this line. $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{b} = (6.6, 8.8)$ matches the closest point from the last lesson.

screens.title: Where P comes from
screens.prose: Times 25, $\mathbf{P}$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 9 & 12 \\ 12 & 16 \end{pmatrix}$. Every entry is a product of two coordinates of $\mathbf{a}$. Multiply the column $\mathbf{a}$ by the row $\mathbf{a}^T$ to see it.
screens.question: Fill in $\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^T$, a column times a row.

hints.text: A 2 × 1 column times a 1 × 2 row is a 2 × 2 matrix.
The entry in row $i$, column $j$ is $a_i a_j$.
$3 \times 3$, $3 \times 4$, $4 \times 3$, $4 \times 4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Row $i$, column $j$ is coordinate $i$ of $\mathbf{a}$ times coordinate $j$.

byKey.r0c1: Row 1, column 1: $3 \times 3 = 9$. A column times a row gives a matrix, not the number $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a} = 25$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{a}\,\dfrac{\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a}}$, and regrouping the product gives $\mathbf{p} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^T}{\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{b}$. So $\mathbf{P} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^T}{\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a}} = \tfrac{1}{25}\begin{pmatrix} 9 & 12 \\ 12 & 16 \end{pmatrix}$. The top is a matrix and the bottom is a number.

screens.prose: $\mathbf{p} = (6.6, 8.8)$ is already on the line. Project it again.
screens.question: What is $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{p}$?

options.why: You scaled $\mathbf{p}$ by 2.2 again. The 2.2 was the multiple of $\mathbf{a}$ for $\mathbf{b}$, not a factor to reapply.
Nothing of $\mathbf{p}$ is perpendicular to the line, so nothing is removed. $(0, 0)$ is what $\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}$ gives.
You used only the diagonal of $\mathbf{P}$: $0.36 \times 6.6$ and $0.64 \times 8.8$. Each row of $\mathbf{P}$ dots with all of $\mathbf{p}$, so the 0.48 terms count too.

hints.text: Where is the point of the line closest to a point on the line?
Row 1 of $\mathbf{P}$ dotted with $\mathbf{p}$: $0.36 \times 6.6 + 0.48 \times 8.8$.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}$: a point on the line is its own projection.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply out $0.36 \times 6.6 + 0.48 \times 8.8$, or think about where $\mathbf{p}$ already is.

explain.text: $\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{b}$ for every $\mathbf{b}$, so $\mathbf{P}^2 = \mathbf{P}$. Projecting twice is projecting once. Notice also $\mathbf{P}^T = \mathbf{P}$: the matrix is symmetric.

screens.prose: $\mathbf{P}$ keeps the part of $\mathbf{b}$ along the line. $\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}$ keeps what is left: $(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P})\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{e}$.
screens.question: Fill in $\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}$.

hints.text: Subtract entry by entry.
The diagonal of $\mathbf{I}$ is 1 and the rest is 0. So off the diagonal you get $0 - 0.48$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract each entry of $\mathbf{P}$ from the matching entry of $\mathbf{I}$.

byKey.r0c2: Off the diagonal $\mathbf{I}$ has 0, so the entry is $0 - 0.48 = -0.48$.
byKey.r1c1: Off the diagonal $\mathbf{I}$ has 0, so the entry is $0 - 0.48 = -0.48$.

explain.text: $(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P})(5, 10) = (3.2 - 4.8,\ -2.4 + 3.6) = (-1.6, 1.2)$, the error. $\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}$ is itself a projection matrix: it projects onto the perpendicular line, through $(-4, 3)$. It also satisfies $(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P})^2 = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}$.

screens.title: Onto a plane
screens.prose: Now project onto a plane in 3D: the column space of the 3 × 2 matrix $\mathbf{A}$. On a line, the bottom of the formula was the number $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a}$. Here its place is taken by $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$, a 2 × 2 matrix.
screens.question: Compute $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$.

hints.text: Entry $(i, j)$ is column $i$ of $\mathbf{A}$ dotted with column $j$.
Column 1 is $(1, 1, 1)$ and column 2 is $(0, 1, 2)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot each column of $\mathbf{A}$ with each column.

explain.text: Each entry of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ is a dot product of two columns, which is why it is symmetric. With one column it shrinks to the single number $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a}$.

screens.prose: Dividing by $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a}$ becomes multiplying by the inverse, placed in the middle: $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^T$. Here $(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 5 & -3 \\ -3 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, and multiplying out gives the $\mathbf{P}$ shown.
screens.question: Project $\mathbf{b} = (6, 0, 0)$: find $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{b}$.

hints.text: Only the first entry of $\mathbf{b}$ is non-zero.
So $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{b}$ is 6 times the first column of $\mathbf{P}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{b}$ is 6 times the first column of $\mathbf{P}$.

byKey.r2c1: The first column ends in $-\tfrac{1}{6}$, so the third entry is $-1$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{p} = (5, 2, -1) = 5(1, 1, 1) - 3(0, 1, 2)$, so it is in the column space. The error $\mathbf{e} = (1, -2, 1)$ is perpendicular to both columns: $1 - 2 + 1 = 0$ and $0 - 2 + 2 = 0$.

screens.prose: A classmate wants a shortcut for the projection onto $C(\mathbf{A})$, with $\mathbf{A}$ the 3 × 2 matrix from before. They try to simplify the formula.
screens.question: Which matrix projects onto $C(\mathbf{A})$?

options.why: That step needs $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$, and a 3 × 2 matrix has no inverse. With $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{I}$, $(6, 0, 0)$ would be its own projection, yet it went to $(5, 2, -1)$.
$\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ is a 2 × 2 matrix, and there is no dividing by a matrix. Its inverse has to sit in the middle, where the shapes fit.
The shapes do not fit: a 2 × 2 matrix cannot multiply the 3 × 3 matrix $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T$.

hints.text: Check the shape of every factor.
$\mathbf{A}$ is 3 × 2, $(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1}$ is 2 × 2 and $\mathbf{A}^T$ is 2 × 3.
Does a 3 × 2 matrix have an inverse?

feedback.correct: Shapes $(3 \times 2)(2 \times 2)(2 \times 3)$ give a 3 × 3 matrix, and nothing cancels.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the shapes, and remember $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ needs a square matrix.

byKey.cancel: You split $(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1}$ into $\mathbf{A}^{-1}(\mathbf{A}^T)^{-1}$. That rule needs square invertible factors, and $\mathbf{A}$ is 3 × 2.
byKey.divide: You divided by $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ as if it were a number. With two columns it is a matrix: multiply by its inverse, in the middle.

explain.text: The cancelling fails because $\mathbf{A}$ is not square. When $\mathbf{A}$ is square and invertible it is legal, and $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{I}$. That fits: then $C(\mathbf{A})$ is the whole space, and every $\mathbf{b}$ is its own projection.

screens.prose: Why does the inverse sit in the middle? As on a line, the error must be perpendicular to the space, so to every column of $\mathbf{A}$. Assume the columns are independent.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ for some $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$, because $\mathbf{p}$ is in the column space
$\mathbf{A}^T(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \mathbf{0}$, because the error is perpendicular to every column
$\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b}$, multiplying out and moving one term across

hints.text: Start by saying what kind of vector $\mathbf{p}$ is.
Each row of $\mathbf{A}^T$ is a column of $\mathbf{A}$, so $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$ says $\mathbf{e}$ is perpendicular to every column.
Name p, use the right angles, expand, invert, substitute.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name $\mathbf{p}$, use the right angles, then solve for $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$.

byKey.d5: Substituting needs $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$, so that line comes last.

explain.text: The inverse lands in the middle because $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is solved for between $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b}$. With one column, $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ is the number $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a}$ and the formula is the line's again.

screens.title: The hat matrix
screens.prose: Regress three days of a stock's returns $\mathbf{y}$ on an intercept and the market's returns, $(-1, 0, 1)$%. The design matrix has columns $(1, 1, 1)$ and $(-1, 0, 1)$. Its projection matrix $\mathbf{H}$, the **hat matrix**, gives the fitted returns $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}$.
screens.question: Find the fitted returns.

hints.text: Dot each row of $\mathbf{H}$ with $\mathbf{y}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot each row of $\mathbf{H}$ with $\mathbf{y} = (-1, 1.5, 2.5)$.

explain.text: The fitted returns lie on the line $1 + 1.75m$: an alpha of 1% and a beta of 1.75. $\mathbf{H}$ is the same matrix as $\mathbf{P}$ before, because $(1, 1, 1)$ and $(-1, 0, 1)$ span the same plane as $(1, 1, 1)$ and $(0, 1, 2)$. A projection matrix depends only on the space.

ideas: Projection is linear, so a matrix $\mathbf{P}$ does it. Onto a line, $\mathbf{P} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^T}{\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a}}$.
Onto the column space of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^T$, with the inverse in the middle.
$\mathbf{P}^2 = \mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{P}^T = \mathbf{P}$. $\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}$ projects onto the perpendicular space and gives the error.
summary.trap: No dividing by $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$, and no cancelling to $\mathbf{I}$: $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ exists only when $\mathbf{A}$ is square.

quiz.question: Which is the projection matrix onto it?

options.why: That is $\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^T$. Divide by $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a} = 2$.
You divided by $|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{2}$. Divide by $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a} = 2$.
That halves every vector. It sends $(1, -1)$ to $(0.5, -0.5)$, which is not on the line.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build $\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^T$, then divide by $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^T$ is all ones and $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a} = 2$. Check: $\mathbf{P}(1, -1) = \mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbf{P}(1, 1) = (1, 1)$.

quiz.prose: The columns of the 3 × 2 matrix $\mathbf{Q}$ are orthonormal, so $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$.
quiz.question: What is the projection matrix onto $C(\mathbf{Q})$?

options.why: That is the 2 × 2 identity. A projection in 3D must be 3 × 3.
Two columns span only a plane in 3D, so not every $\mathbf{b}$ is its own projection.
A 3 × 2 matrix has no inverse. Put $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$ into the formula instead.

explain.text: The middle factor $(\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q})^{-1}$ is $\mathbf{I}$, so $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^T$. Orthonormal columns remove the inverse, which is why we like them.

quiz.question: Which one is a projection matrix?

options.why: It is not symmetric, and its square is the zero matrix, not itself.
Its square has a 4 in the corner, so $\mathbf{P}^2 \neq \mathbf{P}$. It stretches as well as projecting.
It is not symmetric: it turns vectors as well as shrinking them.

feedback.correct: It is symmetric and equals its own square: it projects onto the $x$-axis.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check $\mathbf{P}^T = \mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{P}^2 = \mathbf{P}$ for each.

explain.text: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ keeps the first coordinate and drops the second: projection onto the $x$-axis. It is symmetric and squares to itself.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf{P}$ projects onto the line through $\mathbf{a} = (1, 2)$, and $\mathbf{b} = (5, 0)$.
quiz.question: What is $(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P})\mathbf{b}$?

options.why: That is $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{b}$. $\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}$ keeps what is left over.
That is $\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{b}$. The error is $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p}$.
Only a $\mathbf{b}$ on the line has zero error. $(5, 0)$ is not a multiple of $(1, 2)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{b}$ first, then subtract it from $\mathbf{b}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 5$ and $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 5$, so $\mathbf{p} = (1, 2)$. Then $(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P})\mathbf{b} = (4, -2)$, which is perpendicular to $(1, 2)$.
